description: Permanent daylight saving time would mean more dark school trips, and Georgia had the largest increase of 14 states. Who answers when a child is hit?
shortAnswer: Darkness does not excuse a driver. O.C.G.A. § 40-6-93 requires every driver to exercise due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian, and to exercise proper precaution upon observing any child. These cases turn on the facts: the speed, the headlights, the phone, and the street lighting.

sections.heading: What the study found
sections.shortAnswer: Permanent daylight saving time would mean at least 2 billion more dark commutes to school. Georgia had the largest increase of those 14 states, with about 71 million more dark trips.

sections.heading: Why this matters in Georgia
sections.shortAnswer: In early January, the sun comes up in Atlanta at about 7:43 in the morning. Under permanent daylight saving time, that would be about 8:43.

sections.heading: “I couldn’t see him”
sections.shortAnswer: Darkness does not excuse a driver. A speed can be too fast for the conditions, even when it is under the limit. O.C.G.A. § 40-6-180.

sections.heading: The stopped bus
sections.shortAnswer: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-163, drivers must stop for a school bus that is loading or unloading with its signals on. Passing a stopped school bus is now a high and aggravated misdemeanor with a fine of at least $1,000.

sections.heading: The bus driver and the school district
sections.shortAnswer: O.C.G.A. § 40-6-164 says a driver who stops to let children off may not move the bus until all children who need to cross the roadway have done so safely. Claims against a public school system are harder.

sections.heading: Can they blame your child, or you?
sections.shortAnswer: Whether your child can be charged with fault depends on age. The law does not require a parent to be perfect.

sections.heading: If your child is hit
sections.shortAnswer: Photograph the scene at the same hour, so the darkness and the lighting are accurate. Keep the clothes and the backpack. Ask for video now.

sections.heading: What parents can do now
sections.shortAnswer: Walk the route with your child in the dark, at the real hour. Put reflective tape on the backpack and the coat, and give your child a small flashlight.

faq.q: Is a Georgia driver liable for hitting a child in the dark at a bus stop?
faq.a: Darkness does not excuse a driver. A driver on a school morning, in the dark, in a neighborhood with a bus stop, knows children may be there. These cases turn on the facts: the speed, the headlights, the phone, the street lighting, and how long that child was there to be seen.

faq.q: Can I sue a Georgia school district if my child is hit at a bus stop?
faq.a: Sovereign immunity protects public schools from most lawsuits. Even at a public school, the courts have treated unloading a child and getting the child to a place of safety as part of operating the bus, so the bus insurance can answer for it.

faq.q: What does the new study say about permanent daylight saving time and school commutes?
faq.a: Permanent daylight saving time would mean at least 2 billion more dark commutes to school in the United States. A fatal crash involving a school-aged pedestrian was roughly twice as likely on dark mornings as after sunrise. It is not a prediction of how many more children would be hit.

faq.q: What evidence should I save if my child is hit walking to the bus stop in the dark?
faq.a: Photograph the scene at the same hour, so the darkness and the lighting are accurate. Keep the clothes and the backpack. Ask neighbors for doorbell and security camera video, because many systems overwrite footage within days.
